case: A 36-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a painless lump in her neck that she noticed 2 months ago. Her father had a thyroidectomy for thyroid cancer at age 41 and later had an adrenal tumor removed. Temperature is 36.8 °C (98.2 °F), pulse is 78/min, respirations are 14/min, and blood pressure is 128/80 mm Hg. Physical examination shows a firm 2.5-cm nodule in the right thyroid lobe and an enlarged right cervical lymph node. Serum studies show a calcitonin concentration of 1,450 pg/mL (normal under 5), calcium 11.0 mg/dL (normal 8.5 to 10.5), and PTH 88 pg/mL (normal 10 to 65). Plasma free metanephrines are within the reference range. Fine-needle aspiration shows polygonal and spindle-shaped cells in an amorphous eosinophilic stroma. Diagnosis: medullary thyroid carcinoma in multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2A.

questions.stem: Congo red staining of the stroma in the aspirate shows apple-green birefringence under polarized light. This material is most likely derived from which of the following proteins?
approach: Apple-green birefringence with Congo red identifies amyloid.
Medullary carcinoma is a tumor of parafollicular C cells, which secrete calcitonin.
In this tumor the amyloid is formed locally from the hormone the tumor cells make.
questions.why: Medullary thyroid carcinoma arises from parafollicular C cells, which make calcitonin. The tumor secretes large amounts of calcitonin, and altered calcitonin molecules fold into amyloid fibrils that collect in the stroma. This is a localized endocrine amyloid, so it does not point to a systemic amyloid disease. Her very high serum calcitonin is the same product measured in the blood and is used as a tumor marker.
whyNot: Light chain (AL) amyloid comes from a plasma cell clone, as in multiple myeloma, and deposits in many organs. It is the wrong source for amyloid inside a C cell tumor.
Serum amyloid A is an acute-phase reactant that forms AA amyloid in long-standing inflammation, such as rheumatoid arthritis or chronic infection.
Correct.
Transthyretin forms amyloid in senile cardiac amyloidosis and in familial amyloid polyneuropathy, not in an endocrine tumor.

questions.stem: Genetic testing shows a heterozygous germline mutation that she shares with her father. Which of the following best explains how a single inherited mutant allele drives C cell hyperplasia and carcinoma in this syndrome?
options: Gain-of-function mutation in the RET tyrosine kinase
Loss-of-function mutation in menin with a second hit
Loss-of-function mutation in the VHL tumor suppressor
Gain-of-function mutation in the Gs alpha subunit
approach: Medullary thyroid carcinoma with an adrenal tumor and hyperparathyroidism in a parent fits MEN2A.
MEN2 is caused by mutations in the RET proto-oncogene, which encodes a receptor tyrosine kinase.
An activating mutation in one allele is enough to signal growth, so no second hit is needed.
questions.why: MEN2A and MEN2B are caused by germline activating mutations of RET, a receptor tyrosine kinase. The mutant receptor signals without its normal ligand, so one mutant allele drives cell growth in C cells, chromaffin cells, and parathyroid cells. This is why the syndrome is autosomal dominant with very high penetrance for medullary carcinoma, and why carriers are offered prophylactic thyroidectomy. In contrast, a tumor suppressor needs loss of both alleles in the tumor cell.
whyNot: Correct.
Menin is the tumor suppressor lost in MEN1 (parathyroid, pituitary, and pancreatic tumors). MEN1 is also autosomal dominant, but a tumor forms only after a second hit removes the normal allele.
Loss of VHL causes von Hippel-Lindau disease, with pheochromocytoma, renal cell carcinoma, and hemangioblastomas, but not medullary thyroid carcinoma.
Activating Gs alpha (GNAS) mutations occur in McCune-Albright syndrome and some GH-secreting adenomas. They do not cause C cell tumors.

questions.stem: Immunohistochemical staining of the tumor cells is positive for calcitonin, chromogranin A, and synaptophysin. The tumor cells share their embryologic origin with which of the following cell types?
approach: Chromogranin A and synaptophysin mark neuroendocrine cells.
Thyroid C cells are classically derived from neural crest cells that migrate into the thyroid through the ultimobranchial body.
Pick the other neural crest endocrine cell, which also forms the pheochromocytoma of MEN2A.
questions.why: Parafollicular C cells are classically taught as neural crest derivatives, like the chromaffin cells of the adrenal medulla. Both make secretory granules, so their tumors stain for chromogranin A and synaptophysin. This shared origin helps explain why MEN2A combines medullary thyroid carcinoma with pheochromocytoma. Follicular cells, parathyroid cells, and islet cells come from endoderm, and the adenohypophysis comes from oral ectoderm.
whyNot: Thyroid follicular cells develop from endoderm of the floor of the primitive pharynx at the foramen cecum. Their tumors are papillary and follicular carcinomas.
Parathyroid chief cells come from endoderm of the third and fourth pharyngeal pouches.
The adenohypophysis, including corticotrophs, develops from Rathke pouch, an outgrowth of oral ectoderm.
Correct.

questions.stem: The surgeon plans to examine all of her parathyroid glands during thyroidectomy. Which of the following findings is most likely?
options: A single enlarged gland with three atrophic glands
Chief cell hyperplasia in multiple glands
A single gland with capsular and vascular invasion
Four small glands with fatty replacement of the parenchyma
approach: High calcium with high PTH means primary hyperparathyroidism.
In MEN syndromes every parathyroid cell carries the germline mutation, so several glands enlarge.
A single adenoma is typical of sporadic disease, and carcinoma is rare.
questions.why: Her raised calcium with an inappropriately high PTH is primary hyperparathyroidism. In MEN2A, as in MEN1, all parathyroid tissue carries the inherited mutation, so the usual lesion is hyperplasia of several glands made of chief cells. A sporadic adenoma, by contrast, is one enlarged gland, and the high calcium suppresses the other glands so they look small. Surgeons therefore look at all four glands in MEN patients.
whyNot: One enlarged gland with suppressed, small remaining glands is the picture of a sporadic parathyroid adenoma, the most common cause of primary hyperparathyroidism overall.
Correct.
Capsular and vascular invasion define parathyroid carcinoma, which is rare and usually causes very high calcium levels.

Small, suppressed glands are expected when hypercalcemia comes from a source other than the parathyroids, such as PTH-related peptide, because the high calcium shuts off PTH secretion. Her PTH is high.

dx: Anaplastic thyroid carcinoma arising in a longstanding multinodular goiter
case: A 74-year-old man comes to the physician because of a rapidly enlarging neck mass over the past 6 weeks, with increasing difficulty swallowing and a change in his voice. He has had a goiter for more than 20 years with normal thyroid function and no symptoms other than mild neck fullness. Temperature is 37.0 °C (98.6 °F), pulse is 92/min, respirations are 20/min, and blood pressure is 142/84 mm Hg. Physical examination shows a hard, fixed, 8-cm mass in the left side of a nodular goiter and soft inspiratory stridor. Serum TSH is 1.8 µU/mL (normal 0.4 to 4.0), and free T4 is 1.1 ng/dL (normal 0.8 to 1.8). Core biopsy shows sheets of pleomorphic giant cells and spindle cells with many mitoses and necrosis, invading skeletal muscle. Diagnosis: anaplastic thyroid carcinoma arising in a longstanding multinodular goiter.

questions.stem: Molecular analysis of the tumor is performed. Which of the following genetic changes is most characteristic of this tumor and best explains its loss of differentiation and rapid growth?
approach: Identify the tumor: an older adult with a rapidly growing, invasive, undifferentiated thyroid tumor has anaplastic carcinoma.
Anaplastic carcinoma often arises from a pre-existing differentiated tumor or goiter by gaining further mutations.
The mutation tied to this final step is loss of the guardian of the genome, p53.
questions.why: Anaplastic carcinoma is the most aggressive thyroid cancer. It usually affects people over 60, grows within weeks, invades the trachea, esophagus, and nerves, and most patients die within a year. Many cases arise from a differentiated carcinoma or a longstanding goiter, and inactivating TP53 mutations are the characteristic change in this step to an undifferentiated tumor. Without p53, cells with DNA damage keep dividing, which fits the marked pleomorphism and many mitoses.
whyNot: RET/PTC rearrangements are a hallmark of papillary carcinoma, especially after radiation. They are not what defines the anaplastic step.
PAX8-PPARG fusion is characteristic of follicular carcinoma, which spreads through blood to bone and lung.
Germline RET point mutations cause hereditary medullary carcinoma in MEN2, a C cell tumor of younger patients.
Correct.

questions.stem: A radioiodine scan performed 3 years earlier showed several nodules within the goiter. Which of the following scan features of a nodule is associated with the highest risk of malignancy?
options: Increased uptake with suppression of other tissue
Absent uptake compared with surrounding tissue
Uptake equal to that of surrounding tissue
Diffusely increased uptake in both lobes
approach: Radioiodine uptake shows whether nodule cells still trap iodide and make hormone.
Cancer cells are usually less differentiated and trap little iodide.
So a cold nodule carries more risk than a warm or hot nodule.
questions.why: A euthyroid multinodular goiter has normal TSH and free T4 and usually causes only cosmetic or compressive symptoms. On a radioiodine scan, a nodule that takes up little or no tracer (a cold nodule) has lost the ability to trap iodide, and this group contains most of the cancers. Most cold nodules are still benign, so the next step is fine-needle aspiration. Hot nodules are autonomous and are almost never malignant.
whyNot: A hot nodule that suppresses the rest of the gland is an autonomously functioning nodule. It may cause hyperthyroidism but is rarely malignant.
Correct.
A warm nodule behaves like normal tissue and carries a lower risk than a cold nodule.
Diffusely increased uptake in both lobes is the pattern of Graves disease, not a sign of a malignant nodule.

questions.stem: Laryngoscopy shows that the left vocal fold is immobile in the paramedian position, and his voice is weak and breathy. Tumor invasion of which of the following nerves at which site best explains these findings?
options: Recurrent laryngeal nerve in the tracheoesophageal groove
External laryngeal nerve beside the superior thyroid artery
Internal laryngeal nerve at the thyrohyoid membrane
Ansa cervicalis on the anterior carotid sheath
approach: An immobile vocal fold means paralysis of the intrinsic laryngeal muscles that move it.
All intrinsic laryngeal muscles except the cricothyroid are supplied by the recurrent laryngeal nerve.
This nerve ascends in the groove between the trachea and esophagus, directly behind the thyroid lobe.
questions.why: The recurrent laryngeal nerve runs up in the tracheoesophageal groove, close to the back of each thyroid lobe, and supplies every intrinsic laryngeal muscle except the cricothyroid. When it is invaded or cut, the vocal fold on that side cannot move and rests near the midline, so the voice becomes weak and breathy. Damage to both nerves can close the airway. The same nerve is at risk during thyroidectomy.
whyNot: Correct.
The external laryngeal nerve runs with the superior thyroid artery and supplies the cricothyroid. Injury makes it hard to raise pitch and tires the voice, but the vocal fold still moves.
The internal laryngeal nerve pierces the thyrohyoid membrane and carries sensation from the larynx above the vocal folds. Injury impairs the cough reflex, not fold movement.
The ansa cervicalis supplies the infrahyoid strap muscles. It does not supply laryngeal muscles.

questions.stem: He undergoes palliative total thyroidectomy. Because of a medication error at discharge, levothyroxine is not started. Which of the following patterns of serum TSH and free T4 is most likely 6 weeks later?
options: Low TSH and low free T4
Normal TSH and low free T4
High TSH and low free T4
High TSH and high free T4
approach: Removing the thyroid removes the target gland, so free T4 falls over several weeks.
Low thyroid hormone removes negative feedback on the hypothalamus and pituitary.
A healthy pituitary then raises TSH, giving the primary hypothyroid pattern.
questions.why: T4 has a half-life of about 7 days, so 6 weeks after total thyroidectomy without replacement free T4 is low. The pituitary and hypothalamus are intact, so the loss of feedback drives TSH high. High TSH with low free T4 places the problem in the target gland. This is the same pattern as Hashimoto thyroiditis or iodine deficiency.
whyNot: Low TSH with low free T4 means the pituitary or hypothalamus is failing (central hypothyroidism). His pituitary is normal.
A normal TSH with low free T4 can be seen in central hypothyroidism or severe nonthyroidal illness, but an intact pituitary responds to low T4 by raising TSH.
Correct.
High TSH with high free T4 suggests a TSH-secreting pituitary adenoma or thyroid hormone resistance. He has no thyroid tissue to make T4.

dx: Nonthyroidal illness (euthyroid sick) syndrome in septic shock
case: A 63-year-old woman is admitted to the intensive care unit with septic shock from Escherichia coli pyelonephritis. She has no history of thyroid disease and took no medications before admission. On the fourth hospital day she still requires a norepinephrine infusion. Temperature is 38.6 °C (101.5 °F), pulse is 112/min, respirations are 24/min, and blood pressure is 92/54 mm Hg on norepinephrine. The thyroid gland is not enlarged. Serum studies show a TSH concentration of 1.2 µU/mL (normal 0.4 to 4.0), free T4 1.0 ng/dL (normal 0.8 to 1.8), total T3 42 ng/dL (normal 80 to 180), and reverse T3 56 ng/dL (normal 10 to 24). Diagnosis: nonthyroidal illness (euthyroid sick) syndrome.

questions.stem: Which of the following best explains her low T3 and raised reverse T3?
options: Autoimmune destruction of thyroid follicular cells
Increased thyroxine-binding globulin synthesis in the liver
Reduced hypothalamic TRH with low pituitary TSH output
approach: Note the pattern: low T3, high reverse T3, and normal TSH and free T4 in a critically ill patient.
Most T3 is made outside the thyroid by removing an outer-ring iodine from T4 (5'-deiodination).
The same enzyme activity also clears reverse T3, so less activity lowers T3 and raises reverse T3 together.
questions.why: About 80 percent of circulating T3 is made in peripheral tissues by 5'-deiodinase removing an iodine from the outer ring of T4. Severe illness, cytokines, fasting, and some drugs reduce this activity. Less T4 becomes T3, and reverse T3, which is normally cleared by the same outer-ring deiodination, builds up. TSH usually stays normal, and the pattern reverses as the patient recovers, so it is not treated as thyroid disease.
whyNot: Autoimmune destruction (Hashimoto thyroiditis) lowers free T4 and raises TSH. Her TSH and free T4 are normal.
Correct.
A rise in thyroxine-binding globulin, as in pregnancy, raises total T4 and total T3. Severe illness tends to lower binding proteins instead.
Prolonged critical illness can blunt TRH and TSH, but that would not explain a high reverse T3, and her TSH and free T4 are normal.

questions.stem: Her morning serum cortisol is 34 µg/dL (normal 5 to 23). Which of the following best explains this finding?
options: Increased hepatic synthesis of cortisol-binding globulin
Angiotensin II stimulation of the zona glomerulosa
Autonomous cortisol secretion by an adrenal adenoma
Cytokine-driven release of CRH and ACTH
approach: Sepsis releases large amounts of IL-1, IL-6, and TNF-alpha from activated macrophages.
These cytokines act on the hypothalamus and pituitary to raise CRH and ACTH.
The adrenal responds with more cortisol, which then limits the inflammatory response.
questions.why: During sepsis, IL-1, IL-6, and TNF-alpha stimulate hypothalamic CRH and pituitary ACTH, and the adrenal cortex releases more cortisol. Cortisol then dampens the immune response and supports blood pressure. This loop keeps inflammation from running out of control. A high cortisol in severe illness is an appropriate stress response, not a sign of Cushing syndrome.
whyNot: Cortisol-binding globulin usually falls during severe inflammation and sepsis. A rise would increase total cortisol but would not explain a true stress response.
Angiotensin II stimulates aldosterone from the zona glomerulosa, not cortisol from the zona fasciculata.
An adrenal adenoma would make cortisol without regard to illness. Nothing in her history suggests one, and acute stress fully explains the finding.
Correct.

questions.stem: Deficiency of which of the following trace elements would most directly impair the enzymes whose reduced activity explains her thyroid hormone pattern?
approach: Her pattern comes from reduced deiodinase activity converting T4 to T3.
Deiodinases are selenoproteins with selenocysteine at the active site.
So selenium deficiency impairs T4 to T3 conversion, while iodine deficiency impairs hormone synthesis.
questions.why: The deiodinases that convert T4 to T3 contain selenocysteine in their active site, so they depend on dietary selenium. Low selenium reduces conversion of T4 to active T3. Iodine, in contrast, is the raw material for making T4 and T3 inside the thyroid. Iodine deficiency lowers both hormones, raises TSH, and causes goiter.
whyNot: Iodine deficiency limits synthesis of T4 and T3 in the thyroid, so TSH rises and a goiter forms. It does not act on the deiodinases.
Iron is needed by thyroid peroxidase, a heme enzyme that organifies iodide. Iron deficiency can impair hormone synthesis, not peripheral conversion.
Correct.
Manganese is a cofactor for enzymes such as mitochondrial superoxide dismutase and arginase. It has no role in deiodination.

questions.stem: Her low T3 may blunt her cardiovascular response to catecholamines. Through which of the following actions does T3 normally increase the cardiac response to sympathetic stimulation?
options: Activation of a membrane Gs-coupled receptor
approach: T3 enters cells and binds a nuclear receptor that changes gene transcription.
In the heart, one of the genes it increases is the beta-1 adrenergic receptor.
More receptors mean a larger response to the same level of catecholamines.
questions.why: T3 binds nuclear thyroid hormone receptors and increases transcription of target genes. In heart muscle it increases beta-1 adrenergic receptors and proteins that handle calcium, so heart rate and contractility rise for a given catecholamine level. This is why hyperthyroid patients have tachycardia even though their catecholamine levels are normal, and why beta blockers relieve many symptoms. T3 also raises Na/K-ATPase activity and basal metabolic rate.
whyNot: Correct.
Thyroid hormone acts mainly through intracellular nuclear receptors, not through G protein-coupled receptors on the cell membrane.
Thyroid hormone increases tissue sensitivity to catecholamines. It does not raise adrenal epinephrine output, and catecholamine levels are normal or low in hyperthyroidism.
T3 increases Na/K-ATPase synthesis, which raises oxygen use and heat production. Inhibiting the pump is the action of digoxin.

dx: Cushing disease from a pituitary corticotroph adenoma
case: A 34-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a 1-year history of weight gain, easy bruising, and difficulty climbing stairs. She takes an estrogen-containing oral contraceptive. Temperature is 36.9 °C (98.4 °F), pulse is 84/min, respirations are 14/min, and blood pressure is 154/96 mm Hg. Physical examination shows a rounded face, a dorsocervical fat pad, central obesity with thin extremities, wide purple abdominal striae, and weakness of the hip flexors. Fasting plasma glucose is 142 mg/dL (normal 70 to 99). Late-night salivary cortisol is raised on two occasions. Plasma ACTH is 94 pg/mL (normal 10 to 60). MRI of the brain shows a 6-mm pituitary adenoma. Diagnosis: Cushing disease from a pituitary corticotroph adenoma.

questions.stem: Before the MRI was obtained, which of the following test results would have most strongly favored a pituitary source over ectopic ACTH secretion?
options: No cortisol suppression with low-dose dexamethasone
approach: A high ACTH with hypercortisolism means ACTH-dependent Cushing syndrome: a pituitary adenoma or an ectopic source.
Pituitary corticotroph adenomas keep some sensitivity to glucocorticoid feedback; ectopic tumors usually do not.
So a high dose of dexamethasone lowers cortisol in pituitary disease but usually not with ectopic ACTH.
questions.why: Once hypercortisolism is confirmed, plasma ACTH separates ACTH-dependent from ACTH-independent causes. Her ACTH is high, so the source is a pituitary adenoma or an ectopic tumor such as small cell lung carcinoma. Pituitary adenoma cells still respond partly to strong glucocorticoid feedback, so high-dose dexamethasone usually suppresses cortisol by more than half. Ectopic ACTH-secreting tumors usually do not suppress.
whyNot: Correct.
Failure to suppress with low-dose dexamethasone shows that cortisol excess is present, but it occurs with every cause of Cushing syndrome and does not locate the source.
A suppressed ACTH points to an ACTH-independent cause, such as an adrenal adenoma or exogenous glucocorticoids. Her ACTH is high.
A raised 24-hour urine free cortisol confirms hypercortisolism but does not tell a pituitary source from an ectopic one.

questions.stem: Which of the following tests is most reliable for confirming hypercortisolism in this patient?
approach: Estrogen raises cortisol-binding globulin, which raises total serum cortisol without raising free cortisol.
Any test that measures total serum cortisol can give a falsely high result.
Urine free cortisol reflects only unbound cortisol filtered by the kidney, so binding proteins do not affect it.
questions.why: The three screening tests for Cushing syndrome are 24-hour urine free cortisol, late-night salivary cortisol, and the low-dose dexamethasone suppression test. Estrogen increases hepatic synthesis of cortisol-binding globulin, so total serum cortisol rises even when free cortisol is normal. This can make the dexamethasone test look like a failure to suppress. Urine free cortisol measures only free hormone, so it is reliable in a woman taking estrogen.
whyNot: The overnight dexamethasone test measures total serum cortisol the next morning. Estrogen raises cortisol-binding globulin, so the result can be falsely positive.
A single morning total cortisol is affected by binding globulin, and the morning peak overlaps with normal values. It is a poor screening test.
Correct.
Plasma ACTH is used after cortisol excess is confirmed, to find its source. It does not confirm hypercortisolism.

questions.stem: Which of the following actions of cortisol contributes most to her hyperglycemia?
options: Reduced renal glucose reabsorption by SGLT2
approach: Cortisol is a catabolic, counterregulatory hormone that raises blood glucose.
It breaks down muscle protein and induces hepatic gluconeogenic enzymes.
The amino acids released from muscle feed gluconeogenesis, which also explains her thin limbs and proximal weakness.
questions.why: Cortisol induces hepatic gluconeogenic enzymes such as PEPCK and supplies the substrate by breaking down muscle protein. The liver turns the released amino acids into glucose, while cortisol also reduces glucose uptake in muscle and fat. The result is hyperglycemia, sometimes diabetes. The same muscle breakdown causes her proximal weakness.
whyNot: cAMP-driven glycogenolysis is how glucagon and epinephrine raise glucose within minutes. Cortisol actually increases hepatic glycogen stores.
Correct.
GLUT4 translocation is an action of insulin that lowers blood glucose. Cortisol opposes insulin and reduces glucose uptake.
Reduced SGLT2 reabsorption would increase glucose loss in urine and lower blood glucose. This is how SGLT2 inhibitor drugs work.

questions.stem: She has had two skin infections that healed slowly. Excess cortisol reduces synthesis of both prostaglandins and leukotrienes mainly through which of the following actions?
approach: Both prostaglandins and leukotrienes are made from arachidonic acid.
Arachidonic acid is freed from membrane phospholipids by phospholipase A2.
Blocking that first step cuts off both branches, which is why glucocorticoids suppress both.
questions.why: Glucocorticoids induce annexin A1 (lipocortin) and reduce the expression of inflammatory enzymes, which lowers phospholipase A2 activity. Less arachidonic acid is released from membranes, so both the cyclooxygenase products (prostaglandins) and the lipoxygenase products (leukotrienes) fall. Cortisol also blocks NF-kB, reducing cytokine production. Together these effects weaken inflammation, slow wound healing, and raise infection risk.
whyNot: Acetylation of cyclooxygenase is the action of aspirin. It lowers prostaglandins and thromboxane but not leukotrienes.
Inhibition of 5-lipoxygenase (as by zileuton) lowers leukotrienes only, not prostaglandins.
Leukotriene receptor blockers such as montelukast block leukotriene effects but do not reduce prostaglandin or leukotriene synthesis.
Correct.

dx: Adrenal crisis after abrupt withdrawal of long-term prednisone
case: A 61-year-old man is brought to the emergency department because of 2 days of vomiting, abdominal pain, weakness, and confusion. He has taken prednisone 15 mg daily for 11 months for polymyalgia rheumatica and stopped it 4 days ago when he ran out. Temperature is 37.6 °C (99.7 °F), pulse is 124/min, respirations are 22/min, and blood pressure is 76/42 mm Hg. Physical examination shows a rounded face and no hyperpigmentation of the skin or mucosa. Serum studies show sodium 132 mEq/L (normal 136 to 145), potassium 4.4 mEq/L (normal 3.5 to 5.0), glucose 56 mg/dL (normal 70 to 99), and cortisol 1.6 µg/dL (morning normal 5 to 23). Diagnosis: acute adrenal insufficiency (adrenal crisis) after abrupt withdrawal of long-term prednisone.

questions.stem: Which of the following best explains why stopping prednisone led to adrenal crisis?
options: Bilateral adrenal hemorrhage from consumptive coagulopathy
Autoimmune destruction of all three cortical zones
Fasciculata atrophy from prolonged ACTH suppression
Granulomatous replacement of the adrenal cortex
approach: Long-term prednisone suppresses CRH and ACTH by negative feedback.
Without ACTH, the zona fasciculata atrophies and cannot make cortisol on demand.
Stopping prednisone suddenly removes the only glucocorticoid source, and crisis follows.
questions.why: Supraphysiologic glucocorticoids taken for more than a few weeks suppress hypothalamic CRH and pituitary ACTH. ACTH is the trophic hormone for the zona fasciculata, so the zone atrophies. When prednisone is stopped abruptly, the axis cannot recover fast enough, and the patient develops cortisol deficiency with hypotension, hypoglycemia, vomiting, and confusion. Recovery of the axis can take months, which is why long courses are tapered.
whyNot: Bilateral adrenal hemorrhage causes crisis in sepsis with DIC or with anticoagulation. He has neither, and his history points to steroid withdrawal.
Autoimmune adrenalitis destroys all cortical zones and causes primary insufficiency with hyperpigmentation and hyperkalemia. He has neither.
Correct.
Granulomatous destruction from tuberculosis or histoplasmosis causes primary adrenal insufficiency, usually with hyperpigmentation and hyperkalemia.

questions.stem: Which of the following patterns of plasma hormone concentrations is most likely in this patient?
approach: Prednisone suppresses the pituitary, so this is secondary adrenal insufficiency with low ACTH.
Aldosterone is controlled mainly by the renin-angiotensin system and potassium, not by ACTH.
So aldosterone stays near normal, which matches his normal potassium and lack of hyperpigmentation.
questions.why: In secondary adrenal insufficiency the problem is low ACTH, here from suppression by exogenous glucocorticoid. The zona fasciculata atrophies, but the zona glomerulosa keeps working because angiotensin II and potassium drive aldosterone. That is why hyperkalemia is absent. Hyperpigmentation is also absent because ACTH and other POMC-derived peptides are low.
whyNot: High ACTH with low aldosterone is primary adrenal insufficiency (Addison disease). It causes hyperpigmentation and hyperkalemia, which he lacks.
Low aldosterone would cause hyperkalemia. His aldosterone axis is intact because it does not depend on ACTH.
High ACTH would cause hyperpigmentation and is seen when the adrenal itself fails. Exogenous steroid suppresses ACTH instead.
Correct.

questions.stem: His serum potassium is normal because his aldosterone secretion is intact. Which of the following is the main mechanism by which aldosterone promotes potassium excretion?
options: Principal cell ENaC and potassium channels
approach: Aldosterone acts on mineralocorticoid receptors in the late distal tubule and collecting duct.
In principal cells it increases ENaC sodium channels, Na/K-ATPase, and apical potassium channels.
Sodium entry makes the lumen negative, which drives potassium secretion into the urine.
questions.why: Aldosterone release is driven mainly by angiotensin II and by high plasma potassium. In collecting duct principal cells it increases apical ENaC channels and basolateral Na/K-ATPase. Sodium reabsorption creates a lumen-negative voltage that pushes potassium out through apical potassium channels. Aldosterone also stimulates hydrogen ion secretion by alpha intercalated cells, so its loss causes hyperkalemia with a mild metabolic acidosis.
whyNot: Correct.
The H+/K+ ATPase of alpha intercalated cells secretes hydrogen ions and reabsorbs potassium. It conserves potassium rather than excreting it.
The Na-K-2Cl cotransporter of the thick ascending limb is the target of loop diuretics and is not the main site of aldosterone action.
The proximal tubule Na+/H+ exchanger reabsorbs sodium and bicarbonate. It is driven by angiotensin II, not by aldosterone acting on potassium.

topics: Aldosterone actions in the collecting duct

questions.stem: While he was taking prednisone, his muscle and joint inflammation was well controlled. Which of the following actions of glucocorticoids most directly reduced his production of IL-1, IL-6, and TNF-alpha?
approach: Glucocorticoids bind a cytoplasmic receptor that moves to the nucleus.
The hormone-receptor complex blocks transcription factors that turn on inflammatory genes.
NF-kB is the main transcription factor for IL-1, IL-6, and TNF-alpha.
questions.why: The glucocorticoid-receptor complex enters the nucleus and interferes with NF-kB and AP-1, the transcription factors that switch on genes for IL-1, IL-6, TNF-alpha, and many other inflammatory proteins. Glucocorticoids also induce IkB, which keeps NF-kB in the cytoplasm. In the blood they lower lymphocyte and eosinophil counts and raise neutrophils. These broad effects explain both their benefit in polymyalgia rheumatica and their side effects.
whyNot: Calcineurin inhibition is how cyclosporine and tacrolimus block IL-2 production in T cells. It is not how glucocorticoids act.
Correct.
Neutralizing TNF-alpha is the action of monoclonal antibodies such as infliximab. Glucocorticoids reduce cytokine production rather than binding the cytokine.
mTOR inhibition is how sirolimus blocks T cell proliferation in response to IL-2. It does not describe glucocorticoid action.

dx: Conn syndrome from an aldosterone-secreting adrenal adenoma
case: A 46-year-old man comes to the physician for follow-up of hypertension that remains uncontrolled despite treatment with amlodipine. He reports muscle cramps, weakness, and waking at night to urinate. Temperature is 36.8 °C (98.2 °F), pulse is 76/min, respirations are 14/min, and blood pressure is 168/102 mm Hg. There is no edema. Serum studies show sodium 144 mEq/L (normal 136 to 145), potassium 2.8 mEq/L (normal 3.5 to 5.0), and bicarbonate 32 mEq/L (normal 22 to 28). The plasma aldosterone concentration is raised. CT of the abdomen shows a 1.5-cm nodule in the left adrenal gland, and adrenal vein sampling shows that the excess aldosterone comes from the left side. Diagnosis: Conn syndrome from an aldosterone-secreting adrenal adenoma.

questions.stem: Which of the following additional laboratory findings is most likely and best distinguishes his condition from hypertension caused by renal artery stenosis?
approach: Both primary hyperaldosteronism and renal artery stenosis cause hypertension with high aldosterone and hypokalemia.
In primary disease the adrenal makes aldosterone on its own, so sodium retention and high pressure suppress renin.
In renal artery stenosis the kidney is underperfused, so renin is high and drives aldosterone.
questions.why: In Conn syndrome the adenoma secretes aldosterone autonomously. Sodium retention expands volume and raises pressure at the juxtaglomerular cells, so renin is suppressed. A high aldosterone to renin ratio is the screening test. In secondary hyperaldosteronism, such as renal artery stenosis, low renal perfusion raises renin, which drives the aldosterone. Patients with primary disease rarely have edema because of aldosterone escape.
whyNot: High renin is the hallmark of secondary hyperaldosteronism, as in renal artery stenosis, heart failure, or cirrhosis.
Correct.
Aldosterone excess increases potassium secretion, so urine potassium is inappropriately high despite hypokalemia.
Failure of cortisol suppression with dexamethasone indicates Cushing syndrome. His tumor makes aldosterone, not cortisol.

questions.stem: The left adrenal gland is removed laparoscopically. Which of the following gross findings best supports a cortical adenoma rather than adrenocortical carcinoma?
options: Mass larger than 6 cm with central necrosis
Tumor thrombus extending into the adrenal vein
Mass invading the upper pole of the kidney
approach: Cortical adenomas are small, well-circumscribed, and lipid-rich, so they look yellow.
Carcinomas are large and invasive, with hemorrhage and necrosis.
Choose the feature of a benign, small, lipid-rich tumor.
questions.why: Aldosterone-producing adenomas are usually small, often under 2 cm, encapsulated, and bright yellow on cut section because the cells are full of lipid. Adrenocortical carcinomas are rare, large (often over 6 cm), and invasive, with hemorrhage, necrosis, and spread into veins and nearby organs. Carcinomas are often functional and frequently virilizing. Metastases to the adrenal are more common than primary adrenocortical carcinoma.
whyNot: Correct.
Large size with necrosis suggests adrenocortical carcinoma, not a benign adenoma.
Growth into the adrenal vein or inferior vena cava is a sign of malignancy, seen with adrenocortical carcinoma.
Direct invasion of the kidney is a feature of a malignant tumor. Adenomas stay within their capsule.

questions.stem: Eating large amounts of black licorice can also cause hypertension with hypokalemia. Which of the following findings would best distinguish licorice-induced hypertension from this patient's condition?
approach: Cortisol binds the mineralocorticoid receptor as strongly as aldosterone does.
Renal 11-beta-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase type 2 normally inactivates cortisol to cortisone, protecting the receptor.
Licorice blocks this enzyme, so cortisol acts like aldosterone, and the body lowers its own aldosterone and renin.
questions.why: Mineralocorticoid receptors in the collecting duct bind cortisol and aldosterone equally well, and cortisol circulates at much higher levels. The enzyme 11-beta-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase type 2 converts cortisol to cortisone in these cells, so only aldosterone normally activates the receptor. Glycyrrhetinic acid in licorice inhibits this enzyme. Cortisol then activates the receptor, causing sodium retention, hypertension, and hypokalemia with low renin and low aldosterone. In Conn syndrome aldosterone is high.
whyNot: Licorice does not change pituitary ACTH, and an aldosteronoma does not either, so ACTH does not separate the two.
Both conditions over-activate the mineralocorticoid receptor, so both raise bicarbonate through hydrogen ion secretion.
Both conditions cause hypokalemia through increased potassium secretion by principal cells.
Correct.

questions.stem: On the CT scan, the radiologist notes that the gland containing the nodule differs in shape and position from the gland on the opposite side. Which of the following best describes the normal gland that contains his nodule?
options: Pyramidal gland capping the superior pole of the kidney
Pyramidal gland lying in the lesser sac in front of the pancreas
Crescent-shaped gland on the medial border above the hilum
Crescent-shaped gland lying within the renal capsule at the hilum
approach: The nodule is in the left adrenal gland.
The left gland is crescent shaped and lies along the medial border of the left kidney from the upper pole toward the hilum.
The right gland is pyramidal and sits on the upper pole of the right kidney.
questions.why: Both adrenal glands are retroperitoneal and lie within the renal fascia, separated from the kidneys by perirenal fat. The left gland is crescent shaped and extends along the medial border of the left kidney down toward the hilum. The right gland is pyramidal, caps the upper pole of the right kidney, and lies behind the inferior vena cava. Knowing these shapes helps when reading CT scans and planning adrenal surgery.
whyNot: A pyramidal gland capping the upper pole describes the right adrenal gland, not the left.
The adrenal glands are retroperitoneal, not in the lesser sac. The left gland lies behind the lesser sac and pancreas.
Correct.
The adrenal glands lie outside the renal capsule, in their own compartment of renal fascia, separated from the kidney by fat.

dx: Simple virilizing 21-hydroxylase deficiency with peripheral precocious puberty
case: A 5-year-old boy is brought to the physician because of pubic hair, adult body odor, and rapid growth over the past year. He has never had episodes of vomiting, dehydration, or hospitalization. Temperature is 36.7 °C (98.1 °F), pulse is 92/min, respirations are 20/min, and blood pressure is 98/60 mm Hg. His height is above the 97th percentile. Physical examination shows Tanner stage 3 pubic hair, an enlarged penis, and prepubertal testes with a volume of 2 mL each. Bone age is 9 years. Serum studies show sodium 138 mEq/L (normal 136 to 145), potassium 4.3 mEq/L (normal 3.5 to 5.0), testosterone 150 ng/dL (prepubertal under 10), and 17-hydroxyprogesterone 5,200 ng/dL (normal under 100). Diagnosis: simple virilizing 21-hydroxylase deficiency with peripheral precocious puberty.

questions.stem: His physician also considered 11-beta-hydroxylase deficiency, which also causes virilization. Which of the following steroids accumulates in 11-beta-hydroxylase deficiency, but not in this patient's disorder, and causes hypertension?
approach: 11-beta-hydroxylase acts after 21-hydroxylase, converting 11-deoxycorticosterone to corticosterone and 11-deoxycortisol to cortisol.
Blocking it piles up 11-deoxycorticosterone, a mineralocorticoid.
In 21-hydroxylase deficiency this steroid cannot be formed, so blood pressure is normal or low.
questions.why: In 11-beta-hydroxylase deficiency, high ACTH drives the pathway, and 11-deoxycorticosterone builds up. This steroid activates mineralocorticoid receptors, so patients have hypertension, low renin, and sometimes hypokalemia, together with virilization from shunting to androgens. In 21-hydroxylase deficiency, 11-deoxycorticosterone is not made, so the risk is salt wasting rather than hypertension. The simple virilizing form, as in this boy, keeps enough aldosterone to avoid salt-wasting crises.
whyNot: 17-Hydroxyprogesterone is the substrate of 21-hydroxylase and is the key raised steroid in this boy's disorder. It has no mineralocorticoid effect.
Androstenedione is raised in both disorders and causes virilization, not hypertension.
Corticosterone is made by 11-beta-hydroxylase, so it is low in 11-beta-hydroxylase deficiency. It is raised in 17-alpha-hydroxylase deficiency.
Correct.

questions.stem: A GnRH stimulation test shows LH and FSH responses in the prepubertal range. Which of the following best explains these results together with his small testes?
options: Early activation of the hypothalamic GnRH pulse generator
Activating mutation of the LH receptor in Leydig cells
Constitutive Gs-alpha activation in endocrine tissues
approach: Virilization with prepubertal testes means the androgens are not coming from the testes.
Low LH and FSH show the hypothalamic GnRH pulse generator has not turned on, so this is peripheral precocious puberty.
In congenital adrenal hyperplasia the adrenal makes the androgens, and they suppress GnRH by negative feedback.
questions.why: Central precocious puberty starts with early GnRH pulses, so LH and FSH rise and the testes enlarge. In peripheral precocious puberty, sex steroids come from outside the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis. Here the adrenal glands make androgens under high ACTH drive. These androgens feed back to suppress GnRH, LH, and FSH, so the testes stay small. Years of high sex steroids can later trigger central puberty as well.
whyNot: Early GnRH pulses cause central precocious puberty with pubertal LH and FSH and enlarging testes.
Activating LH receptor mutations (familial male-limited precocious puberty) make the Leydig cells produce testosterone, so the testes usually enlarge, and 17-hydroxyprogesterone would not be high.
Correct.
Constitutive Gs-alpha activation is the cause of McCune-Albright syndrome, with cafe-au-lait spots and fibrous dysplasia. It does not raise 17-hydroxyprogesterone.

questions.stem: His parents are healthy and not related to each other. Genetic testing confirms that he has two mutant CYP21A2 alleles. What is the probability that the parents' next child will be affected?
approach: Congenital adrenal hyperplasia from CYP21A2 mutations is autosomal recessive.
Healthy parents of an affected child must both be carriers.
Two carriers have a one in four chance with each pregnancy of passing on two mutant alleles.
questions.why: 21-hydroxylase deficiency is autosomal recessive and is caused by mutations in CYP21A2, the most common cause of congenital adrenal hyperplasia. An affected child of unaffected parents shows that each parent carries one mutant allele. For each pregnancy, the chance of an affected child is 1 in 4, a carrier 1 in 2, and a noncarrier 1 in 4. Newborn screening measures 17-hydroxyprogesterone to catch affected infants early.
whyNot: 1 in 8 has no basis for two carrier parents; each pregnancy has a fixed 1 in 4 risk.
Correct.
1 in 2 is the risk for the child of a parent with an autosomal dominant disorder, or the chance that a child of two carriers is a carrier.
2 in 3 is the chance that an unaffected sibling of an affected child is a carrier, not the chance of being affected.

questions.stem: Which of the following best explains the high serum testosterone in this patient?
options: Precursor shunting to androgens under high ACTH drive
Increased aromatase conversion of estrogens to androgens
Testicular Leydig cell stimulation by raised LH
approach: 21-hydroxylase deficiency blocks cortisol synthesis, so ACTH rises from lost feedback.
ACTH drives the pathway, and 17-hydroxyprogesterone builds up behind the block.
The 17,20-lyase action of CYP17 turns the excess precursors into androgens, which are then converted to testosterone.
questions.why: 21-hydroxylase converts progesterone to 11-deoxycorticosterone and 17-hydroxyprogesterone to 11-deoxycortisol. When it is blocked, cortisol falls, ACTH rises, and the cortex becomes hyperplastic. Precursors such as 17-hydroxyprogesterone build up and are diverted by 17,20-lyase to DHEA and androstenedione, which are converted to testosterone. The raised 17-hydroxyprogesterone is the diagnostic marker.
whyNot: Correct.
Aromatase converts androgens to estrogens, not the reverse.
11-deoxycortisol is made by 21-hydroxylase, so it is low in this disorder. It is raised in 11-beta-hydroxylase deficiency.
His LH is in the prepubertal range and his testes are small, so the testes are not the source of the testosterone.

dx: Autoimmune Addison disease in autoimmune polyendocrine syndrome type 2
case: A 29-year-old woman comes to the physician because of 4 months of fatigue, a 5-kg weight loss, salt craving, and light-headedness on standing. She has had type 1 diabetes mellitus for 3 years and takes levothyroxine for Hashimoto thyroiditis. Recently she has had frequent hypoglycemia. Temperature is 36.8 °C (98.2 °F), pulse is 104/min, respirations are 16/min, and blood pressure is 94/60 mm Hg supine and 78/50 mm Hg standing. Physical examination shows darkened palmar creases and buccal mucosa. Serum studies show sodium 128 mEq/L (normal 136 to 145), potassium 5.9 mEq/L (normal 3.5 to 5.0), glucose 62 mg/dL (normal 70 to 99), morning cortisol 2.0 µg/dL (normal 5 to 23), and ACTH 520 pg/mL (normal 10 to 60). 21-hydroxylase antibodies are present. Diagnosis: autoimmune Addison disease in autoimmune polyendocrine syndrome type 2.

questions.stem: Which of the following best explains her hyperkalemia?
options: Antibody blockade of renal mineralocorticoid receptors
Loss of zona reticularis androgen production
Loss of zona glomerulosa aldosterone secretion
Loss of medullary epinephrine-driven potassium uptake
approach: Primary adrenal insufficiency destroys the whole cortex, including the zona glomerulosa.
Without aldosterone, principal cells secrete less potassium and reabsorb less sodium.
Hyperkalemia and hyponatremia with volume loss follow.
questions.why: Autoimmune adrenalitis destroys all three zones of the adrenal cortex, so both cortisol and aldosterone fall. Loss of aldosterone reduces sodium reabsorption and potassium secretion in the collecting duct, causing hyperkalemia, hyponatremia, volume depletion, and salt craving. Loss of cortisol adds hypotension and hypoglycemia, and the high ACTH causes hyperpigmentation. In secondary insufficiency aldosterone is preserved, so hyperkalemia does not occur.
whyNot: Antibodies against the mineralocorticoid receptor are not a recognized cause of hyperkalemia. Her 21-hydroxylase antibodies target steroid synthesis in the adrenal cortex.
Loss of adrenal androgens reduces axillary and pubic hair in women but does not affect potassium.
Correct.
The adrenal medulla is spared in autoimmune adrenalitis. Epinephrine shifts potassium into cells through beta-2 receptors, but loss of medullary output is not the cause here.

questions.stem: Autoimmune polyendocrine syndrome type 1 is caused by mutations in the AIRE gene. Which of the following additional findings would have pointed to type 1 rather than type 2 in this patient?
options: Onset of Addison disease in adulthood
approach: AIRE lets thymic medullary epithelial cells show tissue antigens to developing T cells so self-reactive cells are deleted.
AIRE loss causes autosomal recessive APS-1 in childhood: chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis, hypoparathyroidism, and Addison disease.
APS-2 combines Addison disease with autoimmune thyroid disease or type 1 diabetes, usually in adults.
questions.why: AIRE drives expression of tissue-specific self antigens in the thymus so that self-reactive T cells are deleted. Loss of both AIRE copies causes APS-1, which begins in childhood with chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis, then hypoparathyroidism and Addison disease. The candidiasis is linked to autoantibodies against IL-17 and IL-22, which weaken defense against Candida. APS-2 is more common, polygenic and HLA associated, and pairs Addison disease with autoimmune thyroid disease or type 1 diabetes in adults, as in this patient.
whyNot: Autoimmune thyroid disease is a defining part of APS-2, as in this patient, so it does not point to APS-1.
Correct.
Type 1 diabetes is a common component of APS-2 and does not distinguish the syndromes.
Adult onset is typical of APS-2. APS-1 usually begins in childhood.

questions.stem: Loss of cortisol contributes to her hypoglycemia and to a fall in her insulin needs. Which of the following best explains why cortisol raises blood glucose more slowly than glucagon or epinephrine does?
options: Induction of gluconeogenic enzyme gene transcription
Activation of hepatic glycogen phosphorylase by cAMP
Inhibition of insulin release through alpha-2 receptors
Stimulation of muscle glycogenolysis through beta-2 receptors
approach: Glucagon and epinephrine use membrane receptors and second messengers, so they act within minutes.
Cortisol uses an intracellular receptor that changes gene transcription, so its effect takes hours.
Cortisol deficiency removes this slow, sustained support of fasting glucose.
questions.why: During hypoglycemia, glucagon and epinephrine respond first. They act through cell-surface receptors and cAMP to activate glycogen phosphorylase and gluconeogenesis within minutes. Cortisol and growth hormone act over hours. Cortisol binds an intracellular receptor and increases transcription of gluconeogenic enzymes such as PEPCK, and it supplies amino acids from muscle. In adrenal insufficiency this slow support is lost, so a person with type 1 diabetes needs less insulin and has more hypoglycemia.
whyNot: Correct.
cAMP activation of glycogen phosphorylase is how glucagon and epinephrine rapidly break down liver glycogen. Cortisol does not use this pathway.
Alpha-2 inhibition of insulin release is a rapid effect of epinephrine, not of cortisol.
Beta-2 receptor stimulation of muscle glycogenolysis is an epinephrine effect. Muscle lacks glucose-6-phosphatase, so it supplies lactate rather than free glucose.

questions.stem: Which of the following components of her adrenal glands is most likely to be preserved?
options: Lipid-rich cells in radial cords of the middle zone
Small cells in ovoid clusters beneath the capsule
Eosinophilic cells in a network of anastomosing cords
Basophilic chromaffin cells around a central vein
approach: Her 21-hydroxylase antibodies target an enzyme of the adrenal cortex.
Autoimmune adrenalitis destroys all three cortical zones and spares the medulla.
Match each histologic description to its zone, and pick the medulla.
questions.why: In autoimmune adrenalitis, lymphocytes infiltrate and destroy the cortex, which shrinks to a thin rim. The medulla, made of chromaffin cells that secrete catecholamines, is not a target and is preserved. From outside in, the cortex has the zona glomerulosa (ovoid clusters, aldosterone), the zona fasciculata (lipid-rich cells in long cords, cortisol), and the zona reticularis (eosinophilic cells in a network, androgens). The medulla sits in the center around the central vein.
whyNot: Lipid-rich cells in straight cords form the zona fasciculata, which makes cortisol and is destroyed in autoimmune adrenalitis.
Ovoid clusters under the capsule form the zona glomerulosa, which makes aldosterone. Its loss explains her hyperkalemia.
A network of eosinophilic cells forms the zona reticularis, which makes androgens and is also destroyed.
Correct.

case: A 52-year-old man comes to the physician because of 6 months of fatigue, poor appetite, an 8-kg weight loss, and dizziness on standing. Fifteen years ago he was treated for pulmonary tuberculosis but stopped therapy after 2 months. Temperature is 37.4 °C (99.3 °F), pulse is 108/min, respirations are 18/min, and blood pressure is 88/56 mm Hg. Physical examination shows darkened skin over the knuckles and darkened gingiva. Serum studies show sodium 127 mEq/L (normal 136 to 145), potassium 6.0 mEq/L (normal 3.5 to 5.0), morning cortisol 2.4 µg/dL (normal 5 to 23), and ACTH 610 pg/mL (normal 10 to 60). A chest x-ray shows fibrocalcific scarring at the right apex. CT of the abdomen shows enlargement of both adrenal glands with foci of calcification. Diagnosis: Addison disease from tuberculous adrenalitis.

questions.stem: A CT-guided biopsy of an adrenal gland is performed. Which of the following findings is most likely?
approach: Old, incompletely treated tuberculosis with enlarged, calcified adrenals points to tuberculous adrenalitis.
Mycobacterium tuberculosis has a mycolic acid-rich wall that retains carbol fuchsin, so it is acid fast.
The host response forms granulomas with central caseous necrosis.
questions.why: Tuberculosis reaches the adrenals through the blood and destroys the glands with caseating granulomas. The mycolic acids in the cell wall make the bacilli acid fast on Ziehl-Neelsen staining. Infectious adrenalitis enlarges the glands early and leaves calcification later, while autoimmune adrenalitis shrinks them. Tuberculosis is the leading cause of Addison disease worldwide, and it can appear years after the lung infection.
whyNot: Correct.
Small yeasts inside macrophages describe Histoplasma capsulatum, which can also cause adrenalitis. His history of untreated pulmonary tuberculosis makes M. tuberculosis the cause here.
Large cells with intranuclear inclusions describe cytomegalovirus, a cause of adrenalitis in patients with AIDS.
Lymphocytic infiltration with a small, atrophic cortex is autoimmune adrenalitis. His glands are enlarged and calcified.

questions.stem: The biopsy needle is directed toward the right adrenal gland. Which of the following structures lies directly anterior to the medial part of this gland?
approach: The right adrenal gland is pyramidal and sits on the upper pole of the right kidney.
Its medial part lies directly behind the inferior vena cava.
The left gland has different anterior relations, including the pancreas and splenic vessels.
questions.why: The right adrenal gland lies in the retroperitoneum within the renal fascia, on the upper pole of the right kidney. Its medial part lies behind the inferior vena cava, and its lateral part touches the bare area of the liver. Its short vein drains straight into the inferior vena cava, which matters in surgery. The left gland lies behind the stomach, pancreas, and splenic vessels.
whyNot: The aorta lies to the left of the inferior vena cava and is medial to the left adrenal gland, not in front of the right one.
The body of the pancreas lies in front of the left adrenal gland and left kidney.
The left renal vein passes between the aorta and the superior mesenteric artery and receives the left adrenal vein.
Correct.

questions.stem: Two weeks later, during an episode of vomiting, his blood pressure falls to 72/40 mm Hg. It responds poorly to intravenous saline and norepinephrine until hydrocortisone is given. Which of the following actions of cortisol best explains the improved response to norepinephrine?
options: Increased release of ADH from the posterior pituitary
Permissive enhancement of vascular alpha-1 responses
Increased parasympathetic tone to the heart
approach: Norepinephrine raises blood pressure mainly through alpha-1 receptors on vascular smooth muscle.
Cortisol has a permissive effect: it does not constrict vessels itself but is needed for a full catecholamine response.
Without cortisol, vessels respond poorly to pressors, so shock is refractory until cortisol is replaced.
questions.why: Cortisol is permissive for catecholamines. It supports adrenergic receptor expression and signaling in vascular smooth muscle, so norepinephrine and angiotensin II can keep up vascular tone. When cortisol is missing, vessels respond poorly to catecholamines and blood pressure stays low despite fluids and pressors. Giving hydrocortisone restores the response within hours. This is a key reason adrenal crisis presents as shock.
whyNot: Cortisol deficiency increases ADH release, which contributes to hyponatremia. Replacing cortisol lowers ADH rather than raising it.
Correct.
Cortisol reduces prostaglandin synthesis by inhibiting phospholipase A2 and COX-2 expression. More vasodilator prostaglandins would lower pressure.
More parasympathetic tone would slow the heart and lower cardiac output, which would not improve his blood pressure.

questions.stem: Which of the following best explains the darkening of his skin and gingiva?
approach: Low cortisol removes negative feedback, so the pituitary makes much more ACTH.
ACTH is cut from proopiomelanocortin (POMC), which also yields alpha-MSH.
ACTH and MSH stimulate melanocortin 1 receptors on melanocytes, darkening skin creases, scars, and mucosa.
questions.why: In primary adrenal insufficiency, low cortisol releases the pituitary from feedback, and corticotrophs make large amounts of POMC. POMC is cleaved into ACTH and melanocyte-stimulating hormone. Both activate melanocortin 1 receptors on melanocytes and increase melanin. The darkening is most visible in palmar creases, knuckles, scars, and the gums and buccal mucosa. Secondary adrenal insufficiency has low ACTH and no hyperpigmentation.
whyNot: Iron overload in hemochromatosis gives a bronze color, partly from iron and partly from melanin, but his findings are explained by adrenal failure with high ACTH.
Adrenal androgen production falls in Addison disease, and androgens are not the cause of the hyperpigmentation.
Correct.
Carotenoid deposition gives yellow-orange skin, most visible on the palms and soles, with normal sclerae. It is seen with high carrot intake or hypothyroidism and does not darken the gums.

case: An 18-year-old man who lives in a college dormitory is brought to the emergency department because of 12 hours of fever, headache, and a spreading rash. He has not received any meningococcal vaccine. Temperature is 40.0 °C (104.0 °F), pulse is 136/min, respirations are 28/min, and blood pressure is 74/38 mm Hg. Physical examination shows neck stiffness and petechiae and purpura over the trunk and legs. Laboratory studies show a platelet count of 42,000/mm3 (normal 150,000 to 400,000), prothrombin time 24 seconds (normal 11 to 13.5), fibrinogen 90 mg/dL (normal 200 to 400), and a markedly raised D-dimer. Gram stain of cerebrospinal fluid shows gram-negative diplococci. Despite antibiotics, fluids, and vasopressors, he dies 14 hours after arrival. Autopsy shows massive hemorrhage into both adrenal glands. Diagnosis: Waterhouse-Friderichsen syndrome from meningococcemia.

questions.stem: Which of the following best explains the adrenal findings at autopsy?
options: Septic emboli forming bilateral adrenal abscesses
approach: Low platelets, long prothrombin time, low fibrinogen, and high D-dimer mean disseminated intravascular coagulation.
In DIC, small vessels fill with fibrin thrombi while clotting factors and platelets are used up.
In the adrenals, thrombosis plus bleeding causes hemorrhagic necrosis of both glands and acute adrenal insufficiency.
questions.why: In meningococcemia, endotoxin triggers widespread activation of coagulation. Microthrombi block small vessels, and the consumption of platelets and factors causes bleeding. This is the same process that produces the petechial and purpuric rash. In the adrenals the result is bilateral hemorrhagic necrosis, which abruptly ends cortisol and aldosterone production. The resulting acute adrenal insufficiency adds to septic shock and makes it refractory to fluids and pressors.
whyNot: Granulomatous inflammation is caused by tuberculosis or fungi and destroys the adrenals over months, not hours.
Autoantibody-mediated destruction is autoimmune Addison disease, which develops slowly and shrinks the glands.
Septic emboli can form abscesses, but the picture here is diffuse hemorrhage from DIC, not abscess formation.
Correct.

questions.stem: Which of the following components of the organism is most responsible for his shock and disseminated intravascular coagulation?
approach: Gram-negative diplococci in the cerebrospinal fluid of a dormitory resident point to Neisseria meningitidis.
Its outer membrane carries lipooligosaccharide, an endotoxin that activates macrophages and endothelium.
The resulting cytokine release and tissue factor expression cause shock and DIC.
questions.why: Neisseria meningitidis is a gram-negative diplococcus spread by respiratory droplets, which is why close living quarters raise risk. Its outer membrane lipooligosaccharide acts like the lipopolysaccharide of other gram-negative bacteria. It binds TLR4 on macrophages and triggers release of TNF-alpha and IL-1 and expression of tissue factor. These cause vasodilation, capillary leak, and DIC. The organism also sheds outer membrane blebs, so endotoxin levels in the blood become very high.
whyNot: Correct.
The polysaccharide capsule lets the organism resist phagocytosis and survive in blood, and it is the vaccine target, but it does not directly trigger shock and DIC.
IgA1 protease cleaves mucosal IgA and helps colonization of the nasopharynx. It does not cause shock.
Type IV pili attach the organism to nasopharyngeal epithelium. They help colonization, not the systemic inflammatory response.

questions.stem: Which of the following best explains why a polysaccharide-protein conjugate meningococcal vaccine produces class-switched IgG and memory B cells against the capsule?
options: Polysaccharide presented on MHC class I to CD8 T cells
Carrier protein activating complement on the capsule
Carrier peptides recruiting CD4 T cell help
Repetitive epitopes cross-linking B cell receptors
approach: Pure polysaccharides cannot be presented on MHC molecules, so they cause a T cell independent response with mostly IgM and little memory.
In a conjugate, a capsule-specific B cell takes up the whole molecule and presents peptides from the carrier protein on MHC class II.
Helper T cells that recognize those peptides give CD40 ligand and cytokine signals for class switching and memory.
questions.why: Polysaccharide antigens cross-link B cell receptors and activate B cells without T cell help. The response is mostly IgM, short lived, and weak in young children. Linking the polysaccharide to a protein carrier changes this. B cells specific for the capsule internalize the conjugate and present carrier peptides on MHC class II to CD4 T helper cells. The T cells then drive germinal center reactions, class switching to IgG, affinity maturation, and long-lived memory, which protect against invasive meningococcal disease and Waterhouse-Friderichsen syndrome.
whyNot: Polysaccharides are not presented on MHC class I, and CD8 T cells do not provide help for antibody class switching.
Activating complement is not the role of the carrier protein. Its job is to supply peptides that recruit T cell help.
Correct.
Cross-linking of B cell receptors by repeating sugar units is how a plain polysaccharide vaccine works. It gives a T cell independent IgM response with little memory.

topics: T cell dependent and independent antigens

questions.stem: In the normal adrenal gland, blood flows from capsular arteries through cortical sinusoids into the medulla before leaving through a single central vein on each side. Which of the following depends on this direction of flow?
options: Medullary catecholamine stimulation of the zona glomerulosa
Cortisol induction of medullary PNMT for epinephrine
Direct drainage of cortisol into the hepatic portal vein
Delivery of medullary dopamine to the zona fasciculata
approach: Arteries enter at the capsule, so blood passes through the cortex before reaching the medulla.
Medullary chromaffin cells are therefore bathed in blood with very high cortisol.
Cortisol induces PNMT, the enzyme that methylates norepinephrine to epinephrine.
questions.why: Each adrenal gland receives superior arteries from the inferior phrenic artery, middle arteries from the aorta, and inferior arteries from the renal artery. These form a capsular plexus that feeds sinusoids running inward through the cortex to the medulla. Blood leaves through a central vein: the right vein drains into the inferior vena cava, and the left into the left renal vein. Because medullary cells receive cortisol-rich blood, cortisol induces PNMT, which converts norepinephrine to epinephrine. This is why the adrenal medulla is the main source of circulating epinephrine.
whyNot: Blood flows from cortex to medulla, so medullary products do not reach the zona glomerulosa in this way. Aldosterone is controlled mainly by angiotensin II and potassium.
Correct.
Adrenal veins drain to the inferior vena cava on the right and the left renal vein on the left, not into the hepatic portal vein.
Flow runs from cortex to medulla, so medullary dopamine does not reach the zona fasciculata. Cortisol synthesis is controlled by ACTH.
